t: Minimum Time to Break Locks II
o: Breaking locks in some order π, the j-th lock broken (sword factor j) takes ceil(strength[π(j)] / j) minutes, and total time is the sum — the factor increments per lock broken regardless of waiting. So we must find the permutation minimizing Σ_j ceil(s_{π(j)}/j): a classic assignment problem on an n×n cost matrix c[i][j] = ceil(s_i / j) with n ≤ 80. Minimum-cost bipartite matching via successive shortest augmenting paths (SPFA-based MCMF) solves it in O(n) augmentations on a tiny graph.
k: Total time = Σ_j ceil(strength[π(j)] / j) over the chosen order π — waiting never changes the factor sequence.
Minimizing this over all permutations is a linear assignment problem; build cost[i][j] = ceil(s_i / (j+1)) and run min-cost matching.
With n ≤ 80, an MCMF network (source → locks → positions → sink, unit capacities) with SPFA-based successive shortest paths is fast enough.

a.i: Unit-capacity edges S→lock i (cost 0), lock i→position j (cost ceil(s_i/(j+1))), position j→T (cost 0). Augmenting n times along shortest (cheapest) paths yields the minimum-cost perfect matching, which equals the minimum total time.
s: Build the flow network with residual edges
Repeat n times: SPFA for the cheapest augmenting path S→T, add its cost, push 1 unit along it
a.t: O(n · V · E) = O(80 · 162 · ~6600) ≈ 10^8 worst case but far faster in practice (SPFA converges in a few passes per augmentation)
a.sp: O(E) = O(n²) for the residual graph

w: The reduction to assignment is the key leap: verify on [3,4,1] that order (1,4,3) costs 1+2+1=4. A greedy 'sort strengths' fails (sorted-descending gives 7 here), which motivates the matching. Alternatives: the Hungarian algorithm (O(n³)) or, since cost c[i][j]=ceil(s_i/j) is Monge-like, specialized DP — but MCMF is the most reusable template. Pitfall: ceil via integer arithmetic (s + j − 1) // j, i.e., (strength[i] + j) // (j+1) with 0-indexed j.
